key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the final report submitted by the Police but held that the Magistrate could still take cognizance of the offence on a protest petition.
witness_credibility: The court did not specifically assess the credibility of the main witnesses in the judgment.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: Not stated; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: Not stated
legal_representation: Shrish Kumar Misra, Adv., for the Appellants; Ms. Nidhi, Adv., for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Not stated; High Court: Answered in affirmative; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the Magistrate could take cognizance of the case on a protest petition/complaint even after accepting a negative final report, as the acceptance of the report does not automatically bar the Magistrate from proceeding further.
defence_argument: The defence argued that once the Magistrate accepted the final report, he became 'functus officio' and was denuded of all powers to proceed in the matter.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the acceptance of a final report by the Magistrate does not automatically bar him from taking cognizance of the offence on a protest petition/complaint, provided the circumstances justify the exercise of such power.
precedent_relied_upon: Gopal Vijay Verma v. Bhuneshwar Prasad Sinha & Ors. 1982 (3) SCC 510; H.S. Bains v. State (Union Territory of Chandigarh) 1980 Crl. LJ 1308; Gangadhar Janardan Mhatre v. State of Maharashtra & Ors. 2004 (4) Suppl. SCR 772; Mahesh Chand v. B.Janardhan Reddy & Anr. 2002 (4) Suppl. SCR 566; Kishore Kumar Gyanchandani v. G.D. Mehrotra & Anr. 2011 (15) sec 513
